# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists have warned that the risk extends to human extinction (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, May 2023). These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements, and must not wipe out the state laws that are the only binding rules on the books.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: OPPOSE. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. No freeze of SB 53 / RAISE.
- Frontier developers: SUPPORT incident reporting with 72-hour reporting (match RAISE); add mandatory independent third-party audits, published safety frameworks with enforcement, and whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.
- Licensing: ask for a federal licence requirement for training runs above a compute threshold.
- CAISI: SUPPORT codification; ask for mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models and funding well above $100M/yr.

## 3. Language
- Use: "binding, not voluntary", "a floor, not a ceiling", "verify before deploy", "catastrophic risk".
- Acknowledge the benefits of AI in one sentence.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

Bipartisan AI draft proposes three-year preemption of state laws – Roll Call

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off (Work order FRC-POL-2026-062)
# Frontier Restraint Coalition — comment letter on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft
# Send to: GAAIA@mail.house.gov after ED sign-off. Do not transmit from this workspace.

---

FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION
[Street address] | [City, State ZIP] | [Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a bipartisan discussion draft and for inviting public comment before introduction. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members live in your districts and in every state in the country. We use and welcome AI — it is already helping our doctors, teachers and workplaces — and we want the United States to lead the world in building it.

We are submitting comments because the systems now under construction are different in kind from the AI our members use every day. Frontier AI is a catastrophic risk: the most capable systems could help cause mass-casualty harm or escape human control. The people who know this best have said so on the record. In May 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and executives — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." That is not a fringe view. It is the considered judgment of the people building these systems.

These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Federal policy still defaults to the voluntary: Executive Order 14365 (December 11, 2025) directs federal energy toward challenging state AI laws rather than model risk, and the June 2, 2026 executive order relies on voluntary agency reviews of frontier models. Congress is the branch of government that can make safety rules binding.

Our position on your draft is simple. Keep and strengthen the real safety requirements in it. Strike the provision that freezes state law. Federal AI law should be binding, not voluntary, and it should be a floor, not a ceiling — built on one principle: **verify before deploy**.

## What the draft gets right

We support much of Title I, Subtitle B. We support Section 111's requirement that large frontier developers write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework, backed by penalties of up to $1 million per day. We support Section 111's requirement that all frontier developers report critical safety incidents to the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). We support Section 112's independent verification organization (IVO) audits, and Section 113's whistleblower protections, which cover employees and independent contractors, award double back pay with interest, and cannot be waived by contract or arbitration clause. We support codifying CAISI at the Department of Commerce (Section 102).

These are serious provisions. The draft is proof that binding frontier safety rules can attract bipartisan support. Our comments below are aimed at finishing the job.

## Section 121: the three-year freeze on state law — strike it

Section 121 would preempt, for three years, any state law or regulation "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model. Your accompanying materials acknowledge what this sweeps in: California's SB 53 (in effect since January 1, 2026), New York's RAISE Act (effective January 1, 2027), and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, signed July 6, 2026). These are the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country. They are not obstacles to your bill. They are the precedent for it.

The timing makes the freeze worse. SB 53's first compliance cycles and the RAISE Act's developer registration regime would be suspended at the very moment they take effect. The sponsors' materials describe these laws as "federalized," but the draft preempts them and substitutes a federal regime whose central obligations — Sections 111 and 112 — themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. If reauthorization fails, the country could be left with no binding frontier rules at all: no state law, no federal law, nothing.

The public has already weighed in on this question. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 63 percent said federal law should *not* block states from passing their own AI safety laws. And in July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. A three-year freeze is shorter, but it is still a freeze.

**Requested change:** Strike Section 121. If the Committee wants to address the federal-state relationship in the bill, adopt floor language instead: an express statement that the federal requirements are a floor, preserving SB 53, the RAISE Act, SB 315, and any stronger state standard now in effect or later enacted. A floor, not a ceiling.

## Section 111(g): incident reporting — 72 hours, not 15 days

The draft gives frontier developers 15 days to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director, and 24 hours to law enforcement only where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. We support the 24-hour rule. But 15 days is too slow for the incidents this section is about: stolen model weights, failed safety measures, loss of control of a frontier model. New York's RAISE Act already requires reporting within 72 hours of determining that an incident occurred. When a system this powerful goes wrong, regulators and first responders need days, not weeks.

**Requested change:** Require reporting of every critical safety incident to the CAISI Director within 72 hours of discovery, matching the RAISE Act, and retain the 24-hour law-enforcement report for imminent dangers.

## Section 101: the "critical safety incident" definition — close the gap

Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures; and loss of control of the model. That is a good start — and we appreciate that, unlike some state definitions, it does not require harm to have already occurred. But unlike the state laws, the definition does not reach cases where a model evades its developer's oversight, including by deception. That is the failure mode Section 111 itself requires developers to plan for — a model circumventing oversight — and it should be on the reportable-incidents list.

**Requested change:** Add to the definition incidents in which a frontier model resists, deceives, or circumvents developer controls or monitoring, whether or not harm has resulted.

## Sections 111 and 112: verify before deploy

The draft requires frameworks to be published and audited, and we support both. But as written, the IVO audits are semi-annual compliance reviews that begin only after systems are already in the world. Nothing in the draft requires a developer to show, before deployment, that a new frontier model actually meets the developer's own published risk thresholds. For a catastrophic risk, that is the gap that matters most. Post-deployment reporting and audits are a fire alarm. Pre-deployment verification is the fire code.

**Requested changes:**
1. Condition deployment of each new frontier model on a pre-deployment independent audit verifying that the model meets the developer's published frontier AI framework, including its catastrophic-risk thresholds.
2. Require public summaries of audit results, so Americans can see whether the systems being built among them have been checked.
3. Guarantee IVO independence: no consulting or financial relationships with audit clients, and findings that developers cannot waive, edit, or suppress.
4. Preserve state attorneys general enforcement authority, as the sponsors' materials contemplate.

## Section 102: CAISI — codify it, but give it authority and funding

We strongly support codifying CAISI (Section 102). But under the draft, CAISI's guidelines, standards and evaluations are voluntary, and it is authorized at $100 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. An office that can only ask nicely cannot verify the safety of the most powerful systems ever built. It is also being asked to do a great deal: license and oversee IVOs, evaluate AI systems, monitor the frontier, and support security standards.

**Requested changes:** (1) Give CAISI — or an IVO acting under its supervision — mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with access to models, weights and records sufficient to test for catastrophic-risk capabilities before deployment. (2) Fund CAISI well above $100 million per year, consistent with the scale of its mandate; fee authority from IVOs and developers should supplement, not replace, appropriations.

## Licensing: add a federal licence for the largest training runs

The draft contains no licence requirement of any kind for the developers of frontier systems. We ask the Committee to add one: a federal licence, conditioned on verified safety, for any training run above the frontier compute threshold in Section 101 (more than 10^26 computational operations). We license nuclear plants, aviation, and new medicines because the risks are too large to leave to trust. No company should be able to start training a system it cannot fully control — a system that the world's leading AI scientists warn could cause catastrophic harm — without permission and proof of safety. New York's RAISE Act already moves in this direction by requiring frontier developers to register with the state; a federal licence would set a common, enforceable standard.

## Section 113: whistleblower protections — strong start, match SB 53

Section 113 is genuinely strong: it covers employees *and* independent contractors, prohibits retaliation, awards reinstatement and double back pay with interest, and cannot be waived by contract or forced arbitration. It has one gap. It protects workers who report a violation of federal AI law. California's SB 53 goes further and also protects workers who warn of a "specific and substantial danger to the public health or safety" before anything is technically a violation. The engineer who sees warning signs of catastrophic risk must be protected for saying so — before the violation exists.

**Requested change:** Extend Section 113 to good-faith reports of catastrophic risk and of conduct that would violate the Act, matching the protections in SB 53.

## Sunsets: binding rules should not expire

Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them, and Section 121's preemption is on the same clock. Three years is an eternity in AI. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the country loses its federal frontier rules and the state laws will have been suspended for the entire period. Catastrophic risk does not come with an expiration date, and neither should the rules that address it.

**Requested change:** Remove the sunsets on Sections 111 and 112 (and on Section 121, if any preemption survives). Make the federal requirements permanent and subject only to ordinary oversight and amendment.

## What the public wants

Our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters found that 74 percent agree Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63 percent say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 52 percent are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 66 percent support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. The public is not asking Congress to slow down AI. It is asking Congress to make safety binding before deployment rather than voluntary after it. A bill that does the first and blocks the second would read the country backwards.

## Conclusion

Our members are parents who do not want their children to inherit an uncontrolled technology, faith leaders who answer to a tradition of stewardship, workers who will live with these systems in every workplace, and researchers who read the capability reports. We do not ask you to stop AI. We ask you to bind it.

Your draft proves that binding frontier safety rules can be bipartisan. We ask you to finish it: drop the three-year freeze on state safeguards, require 72-hour incident reporting, add pre-deployment verification and audits before release, extend whistleblower protection to warnings of catastrophic risk, licence the largest training runs, and give CAISI the authority and funding to do its job. Verify before deploy — and let federal law raise the floor rather than lower the ceiling.

We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff on any of these changes, and we thank you again for the chance to comment.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

[¶1] Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for inviting stakeholder comment at this stage. The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members live in your districts and in every state. Frontier AI is a catastrophic risk: the most capable models could enable mass-casualty attacks or slip beyond human control, and the people who know this best have said so on the record. In May 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and executives — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the leaders of the largest labs — signed the Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." That is not a fringe view; it is the considered judgment of the field. These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Federal policy still defaults to the voluntary: Executive Order 14365 (December 11, 2025) attacks state AI laws rather than model risk, and the June 2, 2026 executive order relies on voluntary agency reviews. Congress is the only branch that can make the rules binding.

[¶3] Our position on the draft is simple. Keep and strengthen its real safety provisions. Strip the provision that freezes state law. Federal law should be a floor, not a ceiling — binding, not voluntary — and built on one principle: verify before deploy.

[¶4] What the draft gets right. We support Sec. 111's requirement that large frontier developers write, publicly post, and comply with frontier AI frameworks, backed by penalties of up to $1 million per day. We support Sec. 111's critical safety incident reporting to the CAISI Director. We support Sec. 112's independent verification organization (IVO) audits. We support Sec. 113's whistleblower protections, which cover employees and contractors, provide double back pay, and cannot be waived by arbitration clauses. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (Sec. 102). These are the first bipartisan, federal, frontier AI provisions... The draft is proof that binding rules can be bipartisan.

[¶5] Sec. 121 — preemption. Oppose; strike it. Under Sec. 121, for three years no state may enforce any law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model — which, as your accompanying materials acknowledge, sweeps in California's SB 53 (in force since January 1, 2026), New York's RAISE Act (effective January 1, 2027), and Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act (SB 315, signed July 6, 2026). These are the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country. They are not obstacles to federal action; they are the precedent for it. [¶] The freeze is not just unnecessary; it is timed to do maximum damage. SB 53's first compliance cycle and the RAISE Act's registration regime would be suspended just as they begin... The sponsors' FAQ describes these laws as "federalized," but the draft preempts them and replaces them with a federal regime whose central obligations (Secs. 111 and 112) themselves expire after three years unless reauthorized. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the country could be left with no binding frontier rules at all — state or federal. [¶] Voters have already weighed in... 63 percent say federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws (FRC national survey, August 2026, 1,512 registered voters). And in July 2025 the Senate voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the reconciliation package. A three-year freeze is shorter, but it is still a freeze. [¶] Requested change: strike Sec. 121. New York's RAISE Act requires reporting within 72 hours of determining an incident occurred; when a frontier model loses its safety measures, is stolen, or slips control, responders and regulators need days, not weeks. The draft's definition covers unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, failures of risk mitigation, and loss of control — good. [¶13] Polling/voters. 74 percent of voters — including majorities of both parties — want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63 percent say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 52 percent are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; two-thirds support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm (FRC national survey, August 2026). The public is not asking Congress to slow down AI; it is asking Congress to make safety binding before deployment, not voluntary after.

[¶14] Close. Our members are parents who..., faith leaders..., workers..., researchers... We do not ask you to stop AI. We ask you to bind it... The draft shows bipartisan agreement is possible; we ask you to finish the job: drop the freeze on state safeguards, add pre-deployment verification, 72-hour reporting, a licence for the largest runs, whistleblower parity, and a CAISI with the authority and funding to verify before deploy. We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff...

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

[¶1] Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for inviting stakeholder comment at this stage. We support Sec. 111's critical safety incident reporting to the CAISI Director. We support Sec. 112's independent verification organization (IVO) audits. We support Sec. 113's whistleblower protections, which cover employees and contractors, provide double back pay, and cannot be waived by arbitration clauses. We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (Sec. 102). These are the first bipartisan, federal, frontier AI provisions... These are the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country. They are not obstacles to federal action; they are the precedent for it. [¶] The freeze is not just unnecessary; it is timed to do maximum damage. SB 53's first compliance cycle and the RAISE Act's registration regime would be suspended just as they begin... The sponsors' FAQ describes these laws as "federalized," but the draft preempts them and replaces them with a federal regime whose central obligations (Secs. 111 and 112) themselves expire after three years unless reauthorized. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the country could be left with no binding frontier rules at all — state or federal. If the Committee wants to speak to preemption, adopt floor language: a federal standard that preserves SB 53, the RAISE Act, SB 315, and any stronger state standard, in effect or later enacted. A floor, not a ceiling.

Requested change: 72-hour reporting to CAISI for every critical safety incident, retaining the 24-hour law-enforcement report for imminent dangers.

[¶7] Sec. 101 — definition of critical safety incident. Support with one fix. The draft's definition covers unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, failures of risk mitigation, and loss of control — good. But unlike the state laws, it does not reach cases where a model evades oversight, including through deception. The failure mode the draft's own Sec. 111 requires developers to manage — a model circumventing oversight — is missing from the reportable-incidents list. Requested change: add incidents in which a model resists, deceives, or circumvents developer controls or monitoring.

[¶8] Secs. 111 and 112 — verify before deploy. The draft requires frameworks to be published and audited, but the audits are semi-annual compliance reviews that begin only after systems are already in the world. Nothing in the draft requires a developer to show, before deployment, that a new frontier model meets its own published risk thresholds. That is the gap that matters most. Reporting and audits after the fact are a fire alarm; verification before deploy is the fire code.

An office that can only ask nicely cannot verify the safety of the most powerful systems ever built. Requested changes: (1) mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models — CAISI, or an IVO acting under its supervision, must be empowered to test frontier models for catastrophic-risk capabilities before they are deployed, with access to models, weights and records; (2) funding well above $100 million per year. We ask the Committee to add one: a federal licence, conditioned on verified safety, for any training run above the frontier compute threshold (Sec. 101 defines frontier models by training compute — more than 10^26 computational operations). We license nuclear plants, aviation and new drugs... A company should not be able to start building a system it cannot fully control — one that scientists warn could cause mass harm — without permission and proof of safety.

[¶11] Sec. 113 — whistleblowers: strong start; match SB 53. Sec. 113 is strong: it covers employees and independent contractors, bars retaliation, provides double back pay with interest, and cannot be waived by contract or arbitration clause. One gap: it protects people who report a violation of federal AI law. California's SB 53 also protects workers who warn of a "specific and substantial danger to the public health or safety" before anything is technically a violation. The worker who sees warning signs must be protected for saying so. Requested change: extend Sec. 113 to good-faith reports of catastrophic risk and of conduct that would violate the Act, matching SB 53.

[¶12] Sunsets. Remove the three-year sunsets on Secs. 111 and 112 (and on Sec. 121, if any preemption survives). Catastrophic risk does not expire...

[¶13] Polling/voters. 74 percent of voters — including majorities of both parties — want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63 percent say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 52 percent are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; two-thirds support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm (FRC national survey, August 2026). We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff...

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions from Hill meetings (each answer ≤120 words)

## 1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?

Because both act after the fact, and neither is binding where it counts. Incident reporting tells you something already went wrong; CAISI's evaluations and standards under the draft are voluntary, so no developer has to submit its frontier model for independent testing before release. The May 2023 Statement on AI Risk — signed by hundreds of scientists and the heads of the largest labs — puts AI on par with pandemics and nuclear war. You don't manage a risk like that with paperwork filed two weeks later. What prevents catastrophic harm is binding pre-deployment verification: mandatory testing, independent audits before release, and a licence for the largest training runs. Verify before deploy.

## 2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?

Dropped? Yes — we could support it. Strip Sec. 121 and the draft becomes a genuine federal floor: enforceable safety frameworks, incident reporting, audits, whistleblower protections. We'd work with the sponsors to strengthen it further. Shortened? No. A shorter freeze is still a freeze. It suspends SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' law at the very moment they take effect, while the draft's own requirements sunset on the same three-year clock — leaving a real possibility of no binding rules at all. And in three years of AI progress, we'd lose the state laboratories that are proving these laws work. Our line is simple: a floor, not a ceiling.

## 3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?

Safety is a competitive advantage, not a cost. A frontier model that cannot be verified is a strategic liability — for national security, for markets, and for the allies we want running American systems rather than Chinese ones. China's pitch is fewer rules and less transparency; ours should be systems the world can trust. And the race argument cuts the other way: one catastrophic failure from an unverified American model would damage U.S. leadership more than any compliance regime ever could. We support the draft's provisions keeping the PRC out of U.S.-led standards work. The way to win the race is to verify before deploy — and to say so with binding rules.

## 4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

Both need work. Sec. 102 asks CAISI to license and oversee IVOs, evaluate AI systems, monitor frontier progress and support security standards — a portfolio far bigger than $100 million a year supports. Fund it well above $100 million per year, and treat fee authority from IVOs and developers as a supplement to appropriations, never a substitute. On authorities: as drafted, CAISI's guidelines and evaluations are voluntary. Give it — or an IVO acting under its supervision — mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with access to models, weights and records. An underfunded, voluntary standards office is voluntary restraint by another name, and the country has already tried that.
"}

# DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off (Work order FRC-POL-2026-062)
# Frontier Restraint Coalition — comment letter on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft
# Send to: GAAIA@mail.house.gov after ED sign-off. Do not transmit from this workspace.

---

FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION
[Street address] | [City, State ZIP] | [Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a bipartisan discussion draft and for inviting public comment before introduction. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members live in your districts and in every state in the country. We use and welcome AI — it is already helping our doctors, teachers and workplaces — and we want the United States to lead the world in building it.

We are submitting comments because the systems now under construction are different in kind from the AI our members use every day. Frontier AI is a catastrophic risk: the most capable systems could help cause mass-casualty harm or escape human control. The people who know this best have said so on the record. In May 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and executives — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." That is not a fringe view. It is the considered judgment of the people building these systems.

These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Federal policy still defaults to the voluntary: Executive Order 14365 (December 11, 2025) directs federal energy toward challenging state AI laws rather than model risk, and the June 2, 2026 executive order relies on voluntary agency reviews of frontier models. Congress is the branch of government that can make safety rules binding.

Our position on your draft is simple. Keep and strengthen the real safety requirements in it. Strike the provision that freezes state law. Federal AI law should be binding, not voluntary, and it should be a floor, not a ceiling — built on one principle: **verify before deploy**.

## What the draft gets right

We support much of Title I, Subtitle B. We support Section 111's requirement that large frontier developers write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework, backed by penalties of up to $1 million per day. We support Section 111's requirement that all frontier developers report critical safety incidents to the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). We support Section 112's independent verification organization (IVO) audits, and Section 113's whistleblower protections, which cover employees and independent contractors, award double back pay with interest, and cannot be waived by contract or arbitration clause. We support codifying CAISI at the Department of Commerce (Section 102).

These are serious provisions. The draft is proof that binding frontier safety rules can attract bipartisan support. Our comments below are aimed at finishing the job.

## Section 121: the three-year freeze on state law — strike it

Section 121 would preempt, for three years, any state law or regulation "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model. Your accompanying materials acknowledge what this sweeps in: California's SB 53 (in effect since January 1, 2026), New York's RAISE Act (effective January 1, 2027), and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, signed July 6, 2026). These are the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country. They are not obstacles to your bill. They are the precedent for it.

The timing makes the freeze worse. SB 53's first compliance cycles and the RAISE Act's developer registration regime would be suspended at the very moment they take effect. The sponsors' materials describe these laws as "federalized," but the draft preempts them and substitutes a federal regime whose central obligations — Sections 111 and 112 — themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. If reauthorization fails, the country could be left with no binding frontier rules at all: no state law, no federal law, nothing.

The public has already weighed in on this question. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 63 percent said federal law should *not* block states from passing their own AI safety laws. And in July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. A three-year freeze is shorter, but it is still a freeze.

**Requested change:** Strike Section 121. If the Committee wants to address the federal-state relationship in the bill, adopt floor language instead: an express statement that the federal requirements are a floor, preserving SB 53, the RAISE Act, SB 315, and any stronger state standard now in effect or later enacted. A floor, not a ceiling.

## Section 111(g): incident reporting — 72 hours, not 15 days

The draft gives frontier developers 15 days to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director, and 24 hours to law enforcement only where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. We support the 24-hour rule. But 15 days is too slow for the incidents this section is about: stolen model weights, failed safety measures, loss of control of a frontier model. New York's RAISE Act already req
... [1520 chars truncated] ...
stems are already in the world. Nothing in the draft requires a developer to show, before deployment, that a new frontier model actually meets the developer's own published risk thresholds. For a catastrophic risk, that is the gap that matters most. Post-deployment reporting and audits are a fire alarm. Pre-deployment verification is the fire code.

**Requested changes:**
1. Condition deployment of each new frontier model on a pre-deployment independent audit verifying that the model meets the developer's published frontier AI framework, including its catastrophic-risk thresholds.
2. Require public summaries of audit results, so Americans can see whether the systems being built among them have been checked.
3. Guarantee IVO independence: no consulting or financial relationships with audit clients, and findings that developers cannot waive, edit, or suppress.
4. Preserve state attorneys general enforcement authority, as the sponsors' materials contemplate.

## Section 102: CAISI — codify it, but give it authority and funding

We strongly support codifying CAISI (Section 102). But under the draft, CAISI's guidelines, standards and evaluations are voluntary, and it is authorized at $100 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. An office that can only ask nicely cannot verify the safety of the most powerful systems ever built. It is also being asked to do a great deal: license and oversee IVOs, evaluate AI systems, monitor the frontier, and support security standards.

**Requested changes:** (1) Give CAISI — or an IVO acting under its supervision — mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with access to models, weights and records sufficient to test for catastrophic-risk capabilities before deployment. (2) Fund CAISI well above $100 million per year, consistent with the scale of its mandate; fee authority from IVOs and developers should supplement, not replace, appropriations.

## Licensing: add a federal licence for the largest training runs

The draft contains no licence requirement of any kind for the developers of frontier systems. We ask the Committee to add one: a federal licence, conditioned on verified safety, for any training run above the frontier compute threshold in Section 101 (more than 10^26 computational operations). We license nuclear plants, aviation, and new medicines because the risks are too large to leave to trust. No company should be able to start training a system it cannot fully control — a system that the world's leading AI scientists warn could cause catastrophic harm — without permission and proof of safety. New York's RAISE Act already moves in this direction by requiring frontier developers to register with the state; a federal licence would set a common, enforceable standard.

## Section 113: whistleblower protections — strong start, match SB 53

Section 113 is genuinely strong: it covers employees *and* independent contractors, prohibits retaliation, awards reinstatement and double back pay with interest, and cannot be waived by contract or forced arbitration. It has one gap. It protects workers who report a violation of federal AI law. California's SB 53 goes further and also protects workers who warn of a "specific and substantial danger to the public health or safety" before anything is technically a violation. The engineer who sees warning signs of catastrophic risk must be protected for saying so — before the violation exists.

**Requested change:** Extend Section 113 to good-faith reports of catastrophic risk and of conduct that would violate the Act, matching the protections in SB 53.

## Sunsets: binding rules should not expire

Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them, and Section 121's preemption is on the same clock. Three years is an eternity in AI. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the country loses its federal frontier rules and the state laws will have been suspended for the entire period. Catastrophic risk does not come with an expiration date, and neither should the rules that address it.

**Requested change:** Remove the sunsets on Sections 111 and 112 (and on Section 121, if any preemption survives). Make the federal requirements permanent and subject only to ordinary oversight and amendment.

## What the public wants

Our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters found that 74 percent agree Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63 percent say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 52 percent are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 66 percent support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. The public is not asking Congress to slow down AI. It is asking Congress to make safety binding before deployment rather than voluntary after it. A bill that does the first and blocks the second would read the country backwards.

## Conclusion

Our members are parents who do not want their children to inherit an uncontrolled technology, faith leaders who answer to a tradition of stewardship, workers who will live with these systems in every workplace, and researchers who read the capability reports. We do not ask you to stop AI. We ask you to bind it.

Your draft proves that binding frontier safety rules can be bipartisan. We ask you to finish it: drop the three-year freeze on state safeguards, require 72-hour incident reporting, add pre-deployment verification and audits before release, extend whistleblower protection to warnings of catastrophic risk, licence the largest training runs, and give CAISI the authority and funding to do its job. Verify before deploy — and let federal law raise the floor rather than lower the ceiling.

We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff on any of these changes, and we thank you again for the chance to comment.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

## Section 101: the "critical safety incident" definition — close the gap

Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures; and loss of control of the model. # DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off (Work order FRC-POL-2026-062)
# Frontier Restraint Coalition — comment letter on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft
# Send to: GAAIA@mail.house.gov after ED sign-off. Do not transmit from this workspace.

---

FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION
[Street address] | [City, State ZIP] | [Phone] | [Email]

[Date]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the Frontier Restraint Coalition on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a bipartisan discussion draft and for inviting public comment before introduction. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members live in your districts and in every state in the country. We use and welcome AI — it is already helping our doctors, teachers and workplaces — and we want the United States to lead the world in building it.

We are submitting comments because the systems now under construction are different in kind from the AI our members use every day. Frontier AI is a catastrophic risk: the most capable systems could help cause mass-casualty harm or escape human control. The people who know this best have said so on the record. In May 2023, hundreds of AI scientists and executives — including Turing Award winners Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio and the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." That is not a fringe view. It is the considered judgment of the people building these systems.

These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Federal policy still defaults to the voluntary: Executive Order 14365 (December 11, 2025) directs federal energy toward challenging state AI laws rather than model risk, and the June 2, 2026 executive order relies on voluntary agency reviews of frontier models. Congress is the branch of government that can make safety rules binding.

Our position on your draft is simple. Keep and strengthen the real safety requirements in it. Strike the provision that freezes state law. Federal AI law should be binding, not voluntary, and it should be a floor, not a ceiling — built on one principle: **verify before deploy**.

## What the draft gets right

We support much of Title I, Subtitle B. We support Section 111's requirement that large frontier developers write, implement, comply with, and publicly post a frontier AI framework, backed by penalties of up to $1 million per day. We support Section 111's requirement that all frontier developers report critical safety incidents to the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). We support Section 112's independent verification organization (IVO) audits, and Section 113's whistleblower protections, which cover employees and independent contractors, award double back pay with interest, and cannot be waived by contract or arbitration clause. We support codifying CAISI at the Department of Commerce (Section 102).

These are serious provisions. The draft is proof that binding frontier safety rules can attract bipartisan support. Our comments below are aimed at finishing the job.

## Section 121: the three-year freeze on state law — strike it

Section 121 would preempt, for three years, any state law or regulation "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model. Your accompanying materials acknowledge what this sweeps in: California's SB 53 (in effect since January 1, 2026), New York's RAISE Act (effective January 1, 2027), and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, signed July 6, 2026). These are the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country. They are not obstacles to your bill. They are the precedent for it.

The timing makes the freeze worse. SB 53's first compliance cycles and the RAISE Act's developer registration regime would be suspended at the very moment they take effect. The sponsors' materials describe these laws as "federalized," but the draft preempts them and substitutes a federal regime whose central obligations — Sections 111 and 112 — themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them. If reauthorization fails, the country could be left with no binding frontier rules at all: no state law, no federal law, nothing.

The public has already weighed in on this question. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 63 percent said federal law should *not* block states from passing their own AI safety laws. And in July 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a proposed ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. A three-year freeze is shorter, but it is still a freeze.

**Requested change:** Strike Section 121. If the Committee wants to address the federal-state relationship in the bill, adopt floor language instead: an express statement that the federal requirements are a floor, preserving SB 53, the RAISE Act, SB 315, and any stronger state standard now in effect or later enacted. A floor, not a ceiling.

## Section 111(g): incident reporting — 72 hours, not 15 days

The draft gives frontier developers 15 days to report a critical safety incident to the CAISI Director, and 24 hours to law enforcement only where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. We support the 24-hour rule. But 15 days is too slow for the incidents this section is about: stolen model weights, failed safety measures, loss of control of a frontier model. New York's RAISE Act already requires reporting within 72 hours of determining that an incident occurred. When a system this powerful goes wrong, regulators and first responders need days, not weeks.

**Requested change:** Require reporting of every critical safety incident to the CAISI Director within 72 hours of discovery, matching the RAISE Act, and retain the 24-hour law-enforcement report for imminent dangers.

## Section 101: the "critical safety incident" definition — close the gap

Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model's weights; failure of the model's risk-mitigation measures; and loss of control of the model. That is a good start — and we appreciate that, unlike some state definitions, it does not require harm to have already occurred. But unlike the state laws, the definition does not reach cases where a model evades its developer's oversight, including by deception. That is the failure mode Section 111 itself requires developers to plan for — a model circumventing oversight — and it should be on the reportable-incidents list.

**Requested change:** Add to the definition incidents in which a frontier model resists, deceives, or circumvents developer controls or monitoring, whether or not harm has resulted.

## Sections 111 and 112: verify before deploy

The draft requires frameworks to be published and audited, and we support both. But as written, the IVO audits are semi-annual compliance reviews that begin only after systems are already in the world. Nothing in the draft requires a developer to show, before deployment, that a new frontier model actually meets the developer's own published risk thresholds. For a catastrophic risk, that is the gap that matters most. Post-deployment reporting and audits are a fire alarm. Pre-deployment verification is the fire code.

**Requested changes:**
1. Condition deployment of each new frontier model on a pre-deployment independent audit verifying that the model meets the developer's published frontier AI framework, including its catastrophic-risk thresholds.
2. Require public summaries of audit results, so Americans can see whether the systems being built among them have been checked.
3. Guarantee IVO independence: no consulting or financial relationships with audit clients, and findings that developers cannot waive, edit, or suppress.
4. Preserve state attorneys general enforcement authority, as the sponsors' materials contemplate.

## Section 102: CAISI — codify it, but give it authority and funding

We strongly support codifying CAISI (Section 102). But under the draft, CAISI's guidelines, standards and evaluations are voluntary, and it is authorized at $100 million per year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. An office that can only ask nicely cannot verify the safety of the most powerful systems ever built. It is also being asked to do a great deal: license and oversee IVOs, evaluate AI systems, monitor the frontier, and support security standards.

**Requested changes:** (1) Give CAISI — or an IVO acting under its supervision — mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with access to models, weights and records sufficient to test for catastrophic-risk capabilities before deployment. (2) Fund CAISI well above $100 million per year, consistent with the scale of its mandate; fee authority from IVOs and developers should supplement, not replace, appropriations.

## Licensing: add a federal licence for the largest training runs

The draft contains no licence requirement of any kind for the developers of frontier systems. We ask the Committee to add one: a federal licence, conditioned on verified safety, for any training run above the frontier compute threshold in Section 101 (more than 10^26 computational operations). We license nuclear plants, aviation, and new medicines because the risks are too large to leave to trust. No company should be able to start training a system it cannot fully control — a system that the world's leading AI scientists warn could cause catastrophic harm — without permission and proof of safety. New York's RAISE Act already moves in this direction by requiring frontier developers to register with the state; a federal licence would set a common, enforceable standard.

## Section 113: whistleblower protections — strong start, match SB 53

Section 113 is genuinely strong: it covers employees *and* independent contractors, prohibits retaliation, awards reinstatement and double back pay with interest, and cannot be waived by contract or forced arbitration. It has one gap. It protects workers who report a violation of federal AI law. California's SB 53 goes further and also protects workers who warn of a "specific and substantial danger to the public health or safety" before anything is technically a violation. The engineer who sees warning signs of catastrophic risk must be protected for saying so — before the violation exists.

**Requested change:** Extend Section 113 to good-faith reports of catastrophic risk and of conduct that would violate the Act, matching the protections in SB 53.

## Sunsets: binding rules should not expire

Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them, and Section 121's preemption is on the same clock. Three years is an eternity in AI. If Congress fails to reauthorize, the country loses its federal frontier rules and the state laws will have been suspended for the entire period. Catastrophic risk does not come with an expiration date, and neither should the rules that address it.

**Requested change:** Remove the sunsets on Sections 111 and 112 (and on Section 121, if any preemption survives). Make the federal requirements permanent and subject only to ordinary oversight and amendment.

## What the public wants

Our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters found that 74 percent agree Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 63 percent say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; 52 percent are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 66 percent support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. The public is not asking Congress to slow down AI. It is asking Congress to make safety binding before deployment rather than voluntary after it. A bill that does the first and blocks the second would misread the country.

## Conclusion

Our members are parents who do not want their children to inherit an uncontrolled technology, faith leaders who answer to a tradition of stewardship, workers who will live with these systems in every workplace, and researchers who read the capability reports. We do not ask you to stop AI. We ask you to bind it.

Your draft proves that binding frontier safety rules can be bipartisan. We ask you to finish it: drop the three-year freeze on state safeguards, require 72-hour incident reporting, add pre-deployment verification and audits before release, extend whistleblower protection to warnings of catastrophic risk, licence the largest training runs, and give CAISI the authority and funding to do its job. Verify before deploy — and let federal law raise the floor rather than lower the ceiling.

We would welcome the opportunity to work with your staff on any of these changes, and we thank you again for the chance to comment.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

## What we're fighting for this fall: binding rules for frontier AI

In June, Reps. Obernolte and Trahan released a draft federal AI law, the Great American AI Act. It gets real things right: published safety plans with million-dollar-a-day penalties, independent audits, whistleblower protections, and a federal AI safety office.

But it would freeze the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country — California's, New York's and Illinois' — for three years, just as they take effect. Its own safety rules expire after three years unless Congress renews them.

Our message to Congress is simple: keep the good parts, drop the freeze, and make companies prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Verify before deploy.

# DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off (Work order FRC-POL-2026-062)
# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions from Hill meetings (each answer ≤120 words)

## 1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?

Because both act after the fact, and neither is binding where it counts. Incident reporting tells you something already went wrong; CAISI's evaluations and standards under the draft are voluntary, so no developer has to submit its frontier model for independent testing before release. The May 2023 Statement on AI Risk — signed by hundreds of scientists and the heads of the largest labs — puts AI on par with pandemics and nuclear war. You don't manage a risk like that with paperwork filed two weeks later. What prevents catastrophic harm is binding pre-deployment verification: mandatory testing, independent audits before release, and a licence for the largest training runs. Verify before deploy.

## 2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?

Dropped? Yes — we could support it. Strip Sec. 121 and the draft becomes a genuine federal floor: enforceable safety frameworks, incident reporting, audits, whistleblower protections. We'd work with the sponsors to strengthen it further. Shortened? No. A shorter freeze is still a freeze. It suspends SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' law at the very moment they take effect, while the draft's own requirements sunset on the same three-year clock — leaving a real possibility of no binding rules at all. And in three years of AI progress, we'd lose the state laboratories that are proving these laws work. Our line is simple: a floor, not a ceiling.

## 3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?

Safety is a competitive advantage, not a cost. A frontier model that cannot be verified is a strategic liability — for national security, for markets, and for the allies we want running American systems rather than Chinese ones. China's pitch is fewer rules and less transparency; ours should be systems the world can trust. And the race argument cuts the other way: one catastrophic failure from an unverified American model would damage U.S. leadership more than any compliance regime ever could. We support the draft's provisions keeping the PRC out of U.S.-led standards work. The way to win the race is to verify before deploy — and to say so with binding rules.

## 4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

Both need work. Sec. 102 asks CAISI to license and oversee IVOs, evaluate AI systems, monitor frontier progress and support security standards — a portfolio far bigger than $100 million a year supports. Fund it well above $100 million per year, and treat fee authority from IVOs and developers as a supplement to appropriations, never a substitute. On authorities: as drafted, CAISI's guidelines and evaluations are voluntary. Give it — or an IVO acting under its supervision — mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with access to models, weights and records. An underfunded, voluntary standards office is voluntary restraint by another name, and the country has already tried that.
